content.title: Midwives and women are inseparable
content.summary: AKU-SONAM student celebrates International Day of the Midwife remembers emergency birth situation

media.caption: Mary checks in on one of her patients

content.text: Mary Muchiri, a midwifery student at AKU-SONAM and midwife mentor in a major hospital in Nairobi was sleeping soundly on a hot night in February 2017. Her shift was over and she had shut her eyes to rest in preparation for the new day. At around midnight, she was woken up by the violent vibration of her mobile phone. Who could be calling so late? It was her neighbour, and she was screaming as if her life was in danger.

After asking a few more questions, Mary confirmed that her neighbour needed midwifery assistance that Mary provided to several women daily. She hurried to her neighbour's house and discovered that the neighbour's nanny was giving birth in the toilet. She dashed back to her house and retrieved a pair of gloves, baby wrappers, cotton wool and a plastic paper bag. "By the time I returned, I found that she had already delivered a premature baby. She was just holding the baby helplessly in her hands", says Mary. As warmth is vital for new-borns, Mary covered the infant with baby wrappers and cotton wool. Thereafter, she put some warm water into the plastic bag and carefully held the baby in the warm water to stabilize her temperature and help her breathe before taking the mother and her baby to a hospital.

"The baby was admitted to the new-born unit for three months as she was a pre-term baby who weighed 1.1kgs. She was later discharged and is now a bubbly three-year-old girl. I'm so happy that I was able to keep her alive using improvised items", she says, seeming nostalgic. "Birth is the creation of new families and I enjoy watching women turn into mothers and men into fathers. Sharing such an experience makes you feel like you've known the parents and their babies forever."

Several midwives globally, especially those in developing countries, confront situations that resemble Mary's. They face situations where they have to handle emergency deliveries with teenage mothers amid inadequate resources which forces them to improvise. Additionally, they often have to provide counselling for mothers as well as give sexual reproductive health advice to teenagers and adults who have been abused. In the current uncertain circumstances, midwives continue to risk their lives on the frontline because as Mary says, "women will not wait for the pandemic to end so that they conceive, and those who are pregnant will not wait for the pandemic to end so that they can deliver." This is why every year on the fifth day of May, the world celebrates the International Day of the Midwife, to celebrate midwives as caregivers and advocates of mothers and babies all over the world. Specifically, this year's focus is on how midwives and women can partner to mobilise and unite in achieving gender equality. By ensuring that women deliver safely and by empowering them with information around sexual and reproductive health as well as maternal and child health, midwives play an active role in ensuring gender equality for women all over the world. As Mary likes to say, "Midwives and women are inseparable!" Happy International Day of the Midwife to midwives all over the world!
